segments: Verification scope: nixpkgs nixos-unstable modules and upstream documentation consulted in October 2026. Group membership, package counts, and service defaults change with revisions; when deploying, use the nixpkgs and Home Manager sources locked by your project as the authority. No builds, activations, or desktop runtime tests were performed for this article.
Declarative enablement
Behind these declarations is a whole set of group switches: GNOME on NixOS is split into package groups that can be enabled or disabled independently.
Module group switches (services.gnome.*)
Switch
Default
What it controls
Forced to true
Service foundation: dconf, polkit, accounts-daemon, NetworkManager, xdg portal, power-profiles
Forced to true
GNOME Shell itself: gnome-session + gnome-shell (systemd units), control-center, settings-daemon
Default application suite (for example: nautilus, epiphany, calculator, weather, console…)
Small games (Mines, Sudoku, Chess…)
Developer tools (gnome-builder, dconf-editor, sysprof…)
So:
Minimal GNOME = core-apps.enable = false + exclude gnome-tour/gnome-user-docs (these two are in core-shell optionalPackages, not core-apps)
A more complete GNOME = enable core-apps and the developer tools/games you need (games can remain disabled as appropriate)

The large webkitgtk package
Epiphany, the browser in core-apps, depends on webkitgtk, a very large package that is slow to build/download the first time. A minimal configuration omits it; a full installation comes with that cost.
GDM and the existing login setup
GDM defaults to Wayland; starting with GNOME 50, Wayland cannot be disabled (the option has been removed)
GDM and kmscon are not inherently incompatible: in current nixpkgs, kmscon automatically avoids tty1 when GDM is enabled (the module’s mkIf (!displayManager.enable))

GDM reads registered wayland-sessions/*.desktop files. Hyprland, niri, and similar environments appear on the login screen only when their modules provide sessionPackages. Installing a binary alone does not guarantee that a session is registered.
Use specialisation to define system variants (see Building GNOME Variants with Specialisation), leaving the primary kmscon workflow unchanged
Centralized theme management

Theme packages, dconf settings, and dark-mode scheduling need clear configuration ownership so desktop modules, Home Manager, and external schedulers do not repeatedly write the same key. For example:
home/theme.nix centrally manages GTK theme, icon, and cursor packages, and declares the dconf keys to write during activation.
If a scheduler such as Noctalia switches dark mode at runtime, explicitly give it responsibility for color-scheme, or accept that a later Home Manager activation will restore the declared value.
A GNOME specialisation that inherits the same Home Manager profile can share themes; the user’s HOME and dconf state also remain shared.
This lets multi-desktop configurations reuse theme declarations while making it clear which layer triggers each settings change.
Input method (fcitx5)

GNOME Wayland uses text-input-v3: do not set GTK_IM_MODULE (the official recommendation; GTK uses the native protocol). Use QT_IM_MODULE=fcitx for older Qt versions or applications unable to use the native protocol. Check native protocol support against the actual version of newer Qt releases; XWayland uses XMODIFIERS=@im=fcitx

GNOME Shell limits candidate-window positioning for some toolkit/input-method module paths. You can use the kimpanel extension (pkgs.gnomeExtensions.kimpanel; enable it manually in the Extensions app after installation)
The GNOME module defaults to i18n.inputMethod.type = mkDefault "ibus"; an explicit "fcitx5" setting takes precedence
The practical value of grouping

GNOME’s desktop entry points, service modules, and application lists are declared separately, letting you install default applications, developer tools, or extensions as needed. Modularity makes configuration ownership and dependencies easier to track, but does not prove that one desktop is necessarily more stable than another. When comparing GNOME, COSMIC, or other desktops, record specific versions, login paths, functional requirements, and runtime evidence rather than inferring stability directly from repository organization.
